summary: This proposed standard defines the Structure of Management Information for SNMPv2, which describes how managed objects and MIB modules are written, using a subset of ASN.1. It was replaced by RFC 1902.

plainLanguage.summary: Every thing a network manager can ask about needs a description written in a strict format. This paper says what that format is.

questions: what is the difference between counter32 and gauge32
subtitle: The rules for writing down what a network device can report or be told, using a subset of ASN.1.

tldr.problem: Network management needs every managed object to be described in one precise, shared notation so that managers and devices agree on what each value means.
tldr.mechanism: The Structure of Management Information (SMI) defines a subset of ASN.1 with three macros: MODULE-IDENTITY for modules, OBJECT-TYPE for managed objects and NOTIFICATION-TYPE for unsolicited notifications.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1442 was a Proposed Standard for SNMPv2 and has been obsoleted by RFC 1902.

today: RFC 1442 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1902, so it is no longer the current definition of the SNMPv2 SMI.

sections.title: Purpose of the SMI
sections.content:
Management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects held in a virtual store called the Management Information Base (MIB). The MIB modules are written in a subset of ASN.1, and RFC 1442 defines that subset: the Structure of Management Information (SMI) for version 2 of SNMP.

The SMI has three parts. Module definitions use the MODULE-IDENTITY macro. Object definitions use OBJECT-TYPE. Notification definitions, for unsolicited transmissions, use NOTIFICATION-TYPE.

For exposition, the original framework of RFCs 1155, 1157 and 1212 is called SNMPv1, and the framework described here is SNMPv2.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the rulebook for how to write a description card for each thing a network device can tell you about.

sections.title: Information Modules and the Naming Tree
sections.content:
An information module is an ASN.1 module that defines management information. There are typically three kinds: MIB modules with managed objects, compliance statements, and capability statements for agent implementations. Every module starts with exactly one MODULE-IDENTITY invocation, placed right after any IMPORTS or EXPORTS statements.

Descriptors must be unique and mnemonic, and must not exceed 64 characters. Symbols from other modules are brought in with IMPORTS, and a clash is resolved by writing module.descriptor.

Names live in the OBJECT IDENTIFIER tree whose Internet subtree starts with the prefix 1.3.6.1. Under it, mgmt(2) holds standard objects, experimental(3) holds objects being designed by IETF working groups, and private(4) holds objects defined unilaterally, with enterprises(1) beneath it for vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: All the names are arranged like folders inside folders. Standard things go in one folder, experiments in another and company-specific things in a third.

sections.title: Defining Managed Objects and Their Types
sections.content:
The OBJECT-TYPE macro defines a managed object with a SYNTAX, a MAX-ACCESS (one of not-accessible, read-only, read-write or read-create), a STATUS (current, deprecated or obsolete) and a DESCRIPTION. Optional clauses are UNITS, REFERENCE, INDEX or AUGMENTS, and DEFVAL.

Allowed syntaxes include Integer32, OCTET STRING, OBJECT IDENTIFIER, BIT STRING, IpAddress, Counter32, Gauge32, TimeTicks, Opaque, NsapAddress, Counter64 and UInteger32. A Counter32 increases until it wraps at 4294967295 and starts again from zero. A Gauge32 may go up or down but never exceeds its maximum. A Counter64 may be used only if a Counter32 would wrap in less than one hour. Opaque exists only for backward compatibility and must not be used for new objects.

An OBJECT IDENTIFIER value may have at most 128 sub-identifiers, each no greater than 4294967295.
sections.plainLanguage: Each description card says what kind of value it holds: a plain number, a counter that only goes up, a gauge that goes up and down, or some text. It also says whether you may only look at it or change it too.

sections.title: Tables, Indexes and Notifications
sections.content:
Management operations apply only to scalar objects, but the SMI lets designers imagine conceptual tables. A table has syntax SEQUENCE OF an entry type, and each row is a SEQUENCE of columnar objects. Tables and rows are always not-accessible.

Rows are identified by an INDEX clause, or by AUGMENTS when a new table extends an existing one row for row. A variable-length string index normally uses its length as the first sub-identifier, unless the IMPLIED keyword is given. Scalar objects are identified by appending a sub-identifier of zero. For rows that can be created and deleted, there should be a status column using the RowStatus textual convention with read-create access.

The NOTIFICATION-TYPE macro defines the contents of an unsolicited message. Its OBJECTS clause lists the MIB objects carried in every instance. The RFC's example is a linkUp notification with OBJECTS { ifIndex }.
sections.plainLanguage: A table is like a class roster: each row is one student, and the columns are things like name and grade. The index tells you which row you mean.

sections.title: Revising a Module
sections.content:
When a module is revised, its MODULE-IDENTITY should be updated with a new LAST-UPDATED value and a REVISION and DESCRIPTION pair. The module's label does not change.

Some edits to an object are allowed without renaming it: adding enumerations, moving STATUS from current to deprecated or obsolete, and adding or updating DEFVAL, REFERENCE or UNITS. New columnar objects may be added at the end of a row. Any other change in meaning requires a new OBJECT IDENTIFIER value, and changing a descriptor counts as a semantic change.

The RFC also has an appendix on converting an OSI-style MIB module into this format.
sections.plainLanguage: You may fix typos or add a new page, but if you change what something means you have to give it a brand new name tag.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Its Maximum-access rules are stated as independent of any administrative authorization policy.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper only explains the format of descriptions, so it does not talk about locks and secrets.
